title: Girl With a Sudden Lump in the Neck.

A 12-year-old girl presented with a sudden- and nontraumatic-onset, painless, left-sided neck mass. She had had no
previous surgery. Examination demonstrated a smooth and ﬂuctuant mass palpable in the left supraclavicular region.
Ultrasonographic scan showed a unilocular cyst measuring approximately 7 cm in diameter (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) conﬁrmed a well-circumscribed cystic mass without invasion into the mediastinum (Figure 2). Fine-needle
aspiration yelded approximately 10 mL of milky ﬂuid.
For the diagnosis and teaching points, see page e24.

DIAGNOSIS:
Lymphocele. The diagnosis was conﬁrmed by the high triglyceride concentration of the aspirate.
Although traumatic lymphocele could be due to a sudden weakening of the lymphatic duct wall, consequent
expansion, and cyst formation,1 atraumatic lymphoceles can be due to mild unrecognized trauma or spontaneous
appearance, potentially because of a congenital weakness in the duct wall.2,3 Most patients are asymptomatic, but
compression may lead to dysphagia or dyspnea. The differential diagnosis for such neck masses includes congenital
cysts and tumors. Ultrasonography can conﬁrm the cystic nature of the lesions and MRI helps to deﬁne anatomic
boundaries and potential intrathoracic extension. Fine-needle aspiration may be required for diagnosis.
After 4 ultrasonographically guided sessions of sclerotherapy with sodium tetradecyl sulfate, the cyst desappeared
completely.
